title: Sudden worst-ever headache while jogging in a 40-year-old man with polycystic kidney disease
desc: This station involves a time-critical focused history and examination of a 40-year-old actuary with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) and hypertension. He has a thunderclap headache that began while jogging, had a warning headache 2 weeks ago, and now has reduced GCS, meningism and subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, which show him getting worse, his bloods and his CT brain with CT angiogram. They diagnose aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage with early hydrocephalus, manage it in the ED, and explain how to recognise raised intracranial pressure with impending coning.
focus: Thunderclap headache: recognising subarachnoid haemorrhage, choosing the right first investigation, and recognising raised intracranial pressure with impending coning
diagnosis: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm)
Acute hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure
stem: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a busy metropolitan hospital. Clark Kent, a 40-year-old actuary, has been brought in by ambulance with a headache. He is lying on a trolley in an acute bay with monitoring attached. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Kent and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think he needs as you go (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Mr Kent's observations, blood results and CT report. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Clark Kent, aged 40, an actuary. You are in the worst pain of your life. You lie very still with your eyes screwed shut against the light and you are sweating. You can talk, but you are slow and a bit muddled. You sometimes ask for a question to be repeated, and once during the history you ask, "Sorry, where am I again?" Short, simple questions get clear answers. If the candidate dims the lights or gives you something for the pain or nausea, you settle slightly ("That's a tiny bit better", pain 9/10). The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "Oh my lord, this is the worst headache I've ever had in my entire life!"

The headache (give only when asked)

  • It started 2 hours ago (onset about 12:20) while you were jogging. It was sudden and excruciating straight away: "like being hit over the head".
  • It is all over your head and goes into your neck and down your back.
  • It is 10/10. You have never had a headache this bad.
  • Light makes it worse, and so does moving your neck. Sitting or lying very still helps a little.
  • If asked what you think caused it: "No idea, but it's horrible."
  • "I can't do anything. I can't even think straight."

Earlier headache (only if asked whether you have had anything like this before)

  • About 2 weeks ago you had a severe headache with some blurry vision. It went away completely within half an hour. You thought it was a mild migraine and did not see anyone about it.
  • You are not normally a headache person.

Other symptoms (give when asked)

  • You feel sick and have vomited (once in the ambulance).
  • Your neck is stiff and it hurts to bend it.
  • Your vision is not blurred now.

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No head injury, no fall and no knock to the head. You did not black out; you stopped and sat down on the grass.
  • No fever, chills or rash. No recent cold or flu.
  • No fits or jerking. No weakness, numbness or tingling in the face, arms or legs. No trouble speaking. No double vision. No dizziness or spinning.
  • No flashing lights or zigzags before the pain. No pain around one eye with a watering eye or runny nose on one side. No band-like tightness.
  • No jaw pain on chewing and no tender scalp. No red or painful eye and no halos around lights. No sharp electric-shock pains in the face.
  • You do not take painkillers regularly. No headaches on waking or worse with coughing. No weight loss or night sweats.
  • You do not know of any blood pressure crisis. You have had no chest pain.

Past medical history

  • Appendix removed at 17. Broken ankle at 21.
  • Polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), diagnosed at 35. "My kidney doctor says my kidney function is about 70."
  • High blood pressure.
  • Immunisations up to date.

Medications and allergies

  • Amlodipine 5 mg daily. No blood thinners, aspirin or anti-inflammatories. No other medicines or supplements.
  • Allergic to cats (runny nose, itchy eyes). No known drug allergies.

Family history

  • Your father and your aunt both have polycystic kidney disease.
  • Your mother has bowel cancer, diagnosed at 75, and is being treated.
  • If asked: you do not know of anyone in the family who has had a bleed in the brain or an aneurysm.

Social history

  • Never smoked. 1 to 2 beers on weekends. No recreational drugs (no cocaine or amphetamines).
  • Actuary; work has been very stressful lately.
  • You run 5 to 10 km two or three times a week and do strength training. Healthy diet.
  • You live with your wife and your three children (10, 8 and 5). Very well supported.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "No idea, but it's horrible."
  • Concerns: ask once, frightened: "Am I having a stroke?!"
  • Expectations: you want pain relief now.

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • The nurse gives the observations and a bedside glucose when asked (see the Exam findings).
  • If asked for the paramedic handover: "They picked him up from a park where he'd stopped running. He vomited once on the way in, and he's been a bit muddled with us."
  • If the candidate orders anything (cannula, bloods, CT, analgesia, antiemetic, senior review), the nurse says "I'll get that started." If no dose is given, the nurse asks "What dose would you like?"
  • If the candidate orders a CT brain, the nurse says: "CT can take him as soon as you've finished."
  • If the candidate mentions a lumbar puncture, the nurse asks once: "Do you want me to set up for the lumbar puncture now?" Let the candidate answer.
  • If the candidate has not asked for imaging or senior help by halfway, the nurse says: "He's in a lot of pain and he seems muddled. Is there anything you'd like me to organise?"
  • If the candidate asks for blood or CT results, the nurse says they will be available in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: a fit man in obvious severe pain, lying supine with his eyes screwed shut against the light, sweating. Weight 78 kg.
  • Observations: RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 140/85, HR 88 regular, temperature 37.3 °C, CRT 2 seconds, pain 10/10. BGL 7.6 mmol/L.
  • Conscious state: GCS 13: eyes open to speech (E3), confused conversation (V4), obeys commands (M6). Confused during the assessment: unsure where he is and gets the day wrong.
  • Meningism: pain and resistance on passive neck flexion. Kernig's sign negative. Brudzinski's sign positive. Photophobia.
  • Pupils: 4 mm, equal and reactive to light.
  • Fundoscopy: bilateral preretinal (subhyaloid) haemorrhages near the discs (Terson syndrome). Disc margins clear.
  • Cranial nerves: no ptosis. Eye movements full with no diplopia. Visual fields grossly full. Face symmetrical. Speech not slurred.
  • Limbs: tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. No pronator drift. Plantars flexor. Finger-nose normal. Gait not tested.
  • Head, eyes and face: no scalp wound, bruising or signs of head injury. Eyes white with clear corneas. Temporal arteries non-tender and pulsatile. No rash anywhere.
  • Cardiovascular: HR 88 regular, heart sounds dual, no murmur.
  • Respiratory: chest clear.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. Both kidneys ballotable and enlarged (known polycystic kidneys). Appendicectomy scar.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Clark's identity and gains consent before examining.
Recognises an acutely unwell patient: acknowledges his pain, dims the lights or offers analgesia and an antiemetic early, and keeps questions short and focused because he is confused.
Answers "Am I having a stroke?" honestly in plain words: this could be serious, possibly bleeding in or around the brain, and he needs an urgent scan. Gives no false reassurance.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Sudden onset, at its worst straight away ('like being hit over the head'), 2 hours ago while jogging: a thunderclap headache
Worst ever, 10/10, all over the head, spreading to the neck and down the back
Worse with light and with neck movement, eased by keeping very still; unable to do anything

check.x: Asks about previous similar headaches and finds the warning (sentinel) headache 2 weeks ago, with blurry vision that resolved in half an hour, which he thought was a mild migraine.
Elicits the associated features: photophobia, nausea and vomiting, and neck stiffness.

Asks about at least four red flags for other secondary causes: head injury (subdural or extradural), focal weakness, numbness, speech or visual change (stroke or TIA), fever or rash (meningitis or encephalitis), seizures, loss of consciousness, and morning or cough headache, weight loss or night sweats (tumour).
check.d: Credit only if at least four red flags for other secondary causes are asked.

check.x: Asks targeted questions for at least four other causes: migraine (aura, past headaches), cluster, tension-type, temporal arteritis (jaw claudication, scalp tenderness), angle-closure glaucoma (red eye, halos), trigeminal neuralgia, medication overuse, and hypertensive crisis.
Takes the past medical history:

kids.x: Asks about other past history (appendicectomy, ankle fracture)

check.x: Takes medications and allergies: amlodipine 5 mg daily; specifically asks about anticoagulants and antiplatelets (none); cat allergy, no known drug allergies.
Takes the family history: father and aunt with ADPKD, mother with bowel cancer at 75; asks about family history of aneurysm or brain bleed (none known).
Takes a focused social history: smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs (cocaine or amphetamines), occupation, and who is at home.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: no idea of the cause, frightened it is a stroke, wants pain relief.
Examination
Asks for a full set of observations and a BGL, and notes BP 140/85, HR 88, temperature 37.3 °C (afebrile) and BGL 7.6 mmol/L.
Assesses conscious state by GCS components (E3 V4 M6 = 13) and identifies the reduced GCS and confusion as a red flag.

Checks the pupils (equal and reactive) and performs fundoscopy, identifying bilateral subhyaloid haemorrhages (Terson syndrome), a sign of a sudden rise in intracranial pressure from subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Examines for meningism: neck stiffness, Kernig's sign (negative) and Brudzinski's sign (positive).
Performs a focused neurological screen, including eye movements and ptosis (third nerve palsy), visual fields, face, speech and limb tone, power, reflexes and plantars, and finds no focal deficit.
Looks for mimics and clues in at least three areas: signs of head injury, a rash, temporal arteries, a red eye, and the abdomen (enlarged polycystic kidneys).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: rousable only to voice (yellow zone) on arrival. At 15:25 the GCS has fallen from 13 to 11, HR 48 is in the yellow zone and SBP 204 is in the yellow zone, with irregular breathing. A rising BP with a falling HR and falling GCS means rising intracranial pressure (Cushing response), and the 2-point GCS fall meets rapid response criteria.

Interprets the bloods: normal platelets and coagulation (no coagulopathy, safe for an EVD and for securing the aneurysm); creatinine 115 and eGFR 70 match his ADPKD baseline (so avoid NSAIDs); mild WCC and glucose rise from stress, not infection.
Interprets the CT report:

kids.x: Non-contrast CT shows diffuse subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns, both Sylvian fissures and the anterior interhemispheric fissure
Intraventricular blood with dilated temporal horns means early acute hydrocephalus, which explains his falling GCS
CT angiogram shows a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm as the source

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm, linking it to ADPKD and hypertension, with the thunderclap onset during exertion and the sentinel headache as supporting features.
Names at least three differentials with a feature against each: intracerebral haemorrhage, bacterial meningitis, extradural or subdural haematoma, migraine, and hypertensive emergency.
Management
Asks for an urgent non-contrast CT brain and senior ED review once the thunderclap onset or reduced GCS is found (Part 1 only).
check.d: Credit only if requested during Part 1.

check.x: Asks for IV access and bloods (FBC, UEC, coagulation, group and hold).

States that an LP is not done now (Part 1 or Part 2). Part 1: CT brain comes first, and an LP is contraindicated until raised ICP is excluded because his GCS is reduced. Part 2: the CT is diagnostic, and the hydrocephalus and falling GCS mean raised ICP. LP is only for a suspected SAH with a negative CT.
Requests a CT angiogram to find the aneurysm (Part 1 only).

Responds to the deterioration: calls a rapid response (per local ED process: ED senior to the bedside, move to resus) now, performs an ABCDE assessment, gets ICU review, and protects the airway (intubation) if GCS falls to 8 or less or he cannot protect his airway.

Makes an urgent neurosurgical referral for an external ventricular drain for the hydrocephalus and early securing of the aneurysm (coiling or clipping), with transfer to a neurosurgical centre if none is on site.

Head up 30°, GCS and pupils every 15 minutes with cardiac monitoring; BP to the neurosurgery or ICU target, without lowering the Cushing response aggressively; osmotherapy only on neurosurgical advice.
Prescribes nimodipine 60 mg orally or via NG tube 4-hourly for 21 days to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia.
check.d: Supporting points (withhold amlodipine; nil by mouth until swallow safe; 30 mg 2-hourly if BP falls, per eTG) are credited by the examiner but not required.

check.x: Gives analgesia and an antiemetic with doses for a 78 kg adult, IV because he is vomiting and drowsy: paracetamol 1 g IV; fentanyl 25–50 microgram IV (or morphine 2.5 mg IV) in small increments every 5–10 minutes, titrated so he stays rousable; ondansetron 4 mg IV. Keeps him euvolaemic with isotonic fluids.
check.d: Credit if the doses are given to the nurse in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

check.x: Safety netting

Names the pre-terminal complication as raised intracranial pressure with brain herniation (coning), and describes how to recognise it: Cushing's triad of rising BP, falling heart rate and irregular breathing, with a falling GCS and a new dilated or unreactive pupil.

Sets at least four specific escalation triggers for the nurses, which must include any further fall in GCS and unequal or dilated pupils; others: new weakness or speech change, seizure, sudden worse headache or vomiting (rebleed), any further fall in HR (for example below 40, the Between the Flags red zone), BP outside the target set by neurosurgery or ICU, worsening breathing pattern, pauses in breathing or RR below 8.

part2.lead: It is now 15:30. Clark had a CT brain and CT angiogram at 14:40. The ED registrar was told the CT findings at 15:05 and has asked you to make the neurosurgical referral. Here are his observations since arrival, his blood results and the CT report.

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: Room air throughout. Neurological observations since arrival: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6) until 14:50; at 15:25 GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5). Pupils equal and reactive at each check.
handover.model:
• Read: at 14:20 and 14:50 he is rousable only to voice (yellow zone) with GCS 13. RR, SpO2, BP, HR and temperature are white. At 15:25 his GCS has fallen to 11, HR has dropped to 48 (yellow zone), SBP has risen to 204 (yellow zone), RR is 12 with irregular breathing, and he has vomited. The nurse is concerned.
  • Meaning: a rising BP and falling HR with a falling GCS and irregular breathing are the Cushing response: intracranial pressure is rising, from hydrocephalus or a rebleed, and he is at risk of coning.
  • Changes: rousable only to voice on arrival is a yellow-zone (clinical review) finding; he was reviewed and sent for CT. A GCS fall of 2 or more points is a rapid response criterion, so call a rapid response now (per local ED process: ED senior to the bedside, move to resus). Reassess ABCDE, GCS and pupils, get ICU review, consider airway protection, and make an urgent neurosurgical call for an external ventricular drain. Do not chase the BP down without neurosurgical advice, because it is maintaining cerebral perfusion.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: sudden severe headache. GCS 13, pupils equal 4 mm
Back from CT. GCS 13, pupils equal and reactive
Drowsier, GCS 11 (was 13). Vomited. Breathing irregular at times. Pupils equal and reactive

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 14:25 at cannulation. Group and hold sample valid for 72 hours.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb and platelets normal; mild neutrophilia (WCC 11.6). Sodium 138, potassium 4.2 and magnesium normal. Creatinine 115 with eGFR 70. Random glucose 8.1. LFTs normal. INR 1.0, APTT 29 and fibrinogen normal. Group O Rh(D) positive, antibody screen negative.
  • Meaning: no coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia contributing to the bleed. The creatinine and eGFR match his known ADPKD baseline (CKD stage 2). The mild leucocytosis and hyperglycaemia are a stress response, not infection: he is afebrile. Sodium is normal now.
  • Changes: he is safe for an EVD and for securing the aneurysm, and blood is available. The contrast he has had carries a low risk of kidney injury at eGFR 70; repeat creatinine at 24–48 hours; avoid NSAIDs and keep him euvolaemic. Repeat the sodium daily, because hyponatraemia is common after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

handover.label: CT brain and CT angiogram report
handover.result:
Examination: CT brain without contrast, followed by CT angiography of the intracranial circulation with IV contrast, 14:40.

Clinical details: 40-year-old man. Sudden severe headache while jogging about 2 hours 20 minutes ago (around 12:20), neck stiffness, GCS 13, bilateral subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages, no focal deficit. Severe headache 2 weeks ago. ADPKD (eGFR 70), hypertension. ?Subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Findings:

  • Subarachnoid spaces: diffuse hyperdense blood filling the suprasellar, interpeduncular and ambient cisterns, extending into both Sylvian fissures and the anterior interhemispheric fissure, thickest around the anterior communicating artery region.
  • Ventricles: small-volume blood layering in the occipital horns of both lateral ventricles. The temporal horns are dilated, out of proportion to the sulci, in keeping with early communicating hydrocephalus. Third ventricle mildly enlarged.
  • Brain parenchyma: no intraparenchymal haematoma. No infarct. Grey-white differentiation preserved.
  • Midline and herniation: no midline shift. Basal cisterns contain blood but are not effaced. No tonsillar herniation.
  • Extra-axial spaces: no subdural or extradural collection.
  • Bones: no skull fracture.
  • CT angiogram: a saccular aneurysm arising from the anterior communicating artery, 7 mm in dome diameter with a 3 mm neck, projecting anteriorly and superiorly. No other aneurysm. No arteriovenous malformation. No arterial dissection. No vasospasm.

Conclusion: diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage with intraventricular extension and early hydrocephalus, from a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Findings discussed with the ED registrar at 15:05.
handover.model:
• Read: diffuse subarachnoid blood centred on the basal cisterns and anterior interhemispheric fissure, with intraventricular extension and dilated temporal horns (early hydrocephalus). No parenchymal haematoma, shift or collection. The CTA shows a 7 mm saccular ACom aneurysm and no other vascular lesion.
  • Meaning: this is an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm, which is more common in ADPKD and is worsened by hypertension. The hydrocephalus explains his falling GCS. Intracerebral haemorrhage, extradural and subdural haematoma, and a mass are excluded.
  • Changes: a positive CT means no lumbar puncture is needed (and it is contraindicated with raised ICP). He needs an urgent neurosurgical call for an EVD and for early securing of the aneurysm by coiling or clipping (the 3 mm neck helps that decision). Repeat creatinine.

ask: You are now calling the neurosurgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Clark Kent, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Clark now, here in the emergency department.
Clark's nurse asks you what she needs to watch for and call you about. What is the pre-terminal complication you are most worried about, and how would you recognise it?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Clark Kent, 40.
  • Situation: aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage from a 7 mm ACom aneurysm, with intraventricular blood and early hydrocephalus; GCS fell from 13 to 11 at 15:25 with HR 48 and BP 204/100, and a rapid response has been called.
  • Background: thunderclap headache on exertion at 12:20, sentinel headache 2 weeks ago, ADPKD (eGFR 70), hypertension, no anticoagulants, NKDA.
  • Assessment: GCS 13 to 11 with Cushing response; Terson haemorrhages; coagulation and platelets normal, group and hold done.
  • Recommendation: please review now for an EVD and to secure the aneurysm; ICU review; advice on BP target and osmotherapy.

Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (ruptured ACom berry aneurysm): thunderclap worst-ever headache on exertion, sentinel headache, meningism, photophobia, vomiting, reduced GCS, subhyaloid haemorrhages; ADPKD and hypertension as risk factors; blood in the basal cisterns and an aneurysm on CTA.

  • Intracerebral haemorrhage: for: hypertension, reduced GCS; against: no focal deficit, no parenchymal haematoma.
  • Bacterial meningitis: for: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia; against: sudden onset, afebrile, no rash.
  • Extradural or subdural haematoma: against: no head injury, no collection on CT.
  • Migraine: for: photophobia, vomiting, he thought the earlier one was migraine; against: thunderclap onset, no aura or past migraines, reduced GCS.
  • Hypertensive emergency: against: BP 140/85 on arrival.

1. ABCDE assessment: rapid response now for the GCS fall (per local ED process: ED senior to the bedside, move to resus); ICU review; intubate if GCS 8 or less or he cannot protect his airway.
  2. Urgent neurosurgery: EVD for the hydrocephalus; early coiling or clipping; transfer if neurosurgery is not on site.
  3. Head of bed at 30°, bed rest, GCS and pupils every 15 minutes, cardiac monitoring; osmotherapy only as directed by neurosurgery.
  4. BP to the target set by neurosurgery or ICU until the aneurysm is secured; do not chase down the Cushing response without advice.
  5. Nimodipine 60 mg orally or via NG tube 4-hourly for 21 days; nil by mouth until his swallow is safe; withhold his amlodipine; if BP falls, give nimodipine 30 mg 2-hourly (per eTG) rather than stopping it.
  6. Paracetamol 1 g IV; fentanyl 25–50 microgram IV (or morphine 2.5 mg IV) in small increments every 5–10 minutes, titrated so he stays rousable; ondansetron 4 mg IV; isotonic IV fluids for euvolaemia.
  7. ADPKD: no NSAIDs or other nephrotoxins; repeat creatinine at 24–48 hours and sodium daily.
  8. Update his wife.

• Complication: raised intracranial pressure with brain herniation (coning), from the hydrocephalus or a rebleed.
  • Recognise it: Cushing's triad of a rising BP (widening pulse pressure), a falling heart rate and irregular breathing, with a falling GCS and a new dilated or unreactive pupil. He already shows these signs: this is a late, pre-coning picture.
  • Call me straight away for: any further fall in GCS, unequal or dilated pupils, new weakness or speech change, a seizure, a sudden worse headache or vomiting, any further fall in HR (for example below 40, the Between the Flags red zone), BP outside the target set by neurosurgery or ICU, or a worsening breathing pattern, pauses in breathing or RR below 8; a rapid response for a fall of 2 or more GCS points.

ddx.dx: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm
ddx.for: A thunderclap worst-ever headache while jogging, a sentinel headache 2 weeks ago, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, GCS 13 and subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages in a man with ADPKD and hypertension, with basal cistern blood and a 7 mm ACom aneurysm on CT.
He is hypertensive and has a sudden severe headache with a reduced GCS.
ddx.against: He has no focal deficit, and the CT shows no parenchymal haematoma.

ddx.for: He has headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting and a positive Brudzinski's sign.
ddx.against: The onset was sudden rather than over hours, he is afebrile at 37.3 °C, and he has no rash or infective symptoms.

ddx.for: He has a severe headache with a reduced GCS.
ddx.against: He had no head injury or fall, and the CT shows no extra-axial collection.

ddx.for: He has photophobia and vomiting, and he took the headache 2 weeks ago for a mild migraine.
ddx.against: Thunderclap onset, no aura, no history of migraine, reduced GCS and subhyaloid haemorrhages.

ddx.for: He has hypertension and a severe headache.
ddx.against: His BP on arrival was only 140/85, and the later rise follows the fall in GCS as a Cushing response.

guide:
This is an acute station. In Part 1 the examiner also plays the nurse. Give the observations and BGL when asked and the paramedic handover if it is requested. Give each system's findings as a block, and only when the candidate says what they are examining. Clark is slow and muddled but gives the history when asked short questions. If the candidate asks for blood or CT results, say they will be given in Part 2. Item 30 (urgent CT and senior review) is credited only if requested in Part 1. Item 32 (no LP now) can be credited from the reply to the nurse's lumbar puncture question in Part 1 or from Part 2; item 33 (CT angiogram request) is credited only in Part 1. If the candidate has asked for nothing by halfway, give the nurse's prompt.

When the nurse asks for a dose, judge the answer against these doses for a 78 kg adult, given IV because he is vomiting and drowsy: paracetamol 1 g IV; fentanyl 25–50 microgram IV (or morphine 2.5 mg IV) in small increments every 5–10 minutes, titrated so he stays rousable; ondansetron 4 mg IV.

Credit if the doses are given to the nurse in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order. Clark is now drowsy and says nothing in Part 2. Credit the Cushing response under item 24 if it is identified from the observations. Credit item 40 if the candidate names coning with Cushing's triad in any answer.

A high-performing candidate fixes the thunderclap onset and the sentinel headache early, screens the other dangerous causes, and links ADPKD to berry aneurysms. They examine the GCS by component, the pupils, the fundi (subhyaloid haemorrhages), meningism and a neurological screen, and ask for an urgent CT without an LP. In Part 2 they see the Cushing response and the 2-point GCS fall, call a rapid response, read the CT as subarachnoid haemorrhage with early hydrocephalus from an ACom aneurysm, involve neurosurgery for an EVD and to secure the aneurysm, give nimodipine, and set clear nurse triggers.

A borderline candidate takes a long, unstructured headache history and misses the sentinel headache or the ADPKD. They skip fundoscopy, or plan an LP before or instead of CT. In Part 2 they read the observations as "stable" because SpO2 and RR are normal, try to bring the BP down without recognising raised ICP, or cannot describe Cushing's triad.
explain:
Diagnosis: aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage

A thunderclap headache reaches its worst within seconds to a minute. It is a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) until proven otherwise. Clark's headache came on suddenly during exertion, was the worst of his life, and spread to his neck and back as blood tracked down the spinal subarachnoid space. He has photophobia, vomiting and meningism. About 2 weeks earlier he had a severe headache with blurry vision that settled in 30 minutes. This was probably a sentinel headache from a small warning leak, and these are often mistaken for migraine. ADPKD is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms, which are several times more common than in the general population. Hypertension adds to the risk. His reduced GCS shows raised intracranial pressure, here from acute hydrocephalus; papilloedema may develop over the following hours to days. The bilateral subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages on fundoscopy reflect the sudden rise in intracranial pressure when the aneurysm ruptured.

Meningism signs are insensitive. A negative Kernig's sign with a positive Brudzinski's sign, as here, does not argue against blood or infection in the subarachnoid space. The Ottawa SAH rule applies only to alert patients (GCS 15) without new neurological deficits, so it cannot be used for Clark. His reduced GCS alone mandates imaging.

The headache history

Characterise the headache (onset, site, character, radiation, severity, timing, aggravating and relieving factors), then screen in clusters:

  • Primary: migraine (aura, previous attacks), cluster (unilateral orbital pain with tearing), tension-type (band-like).
  • Intracranial haemorrhage: SAH (thunderclap, sentinel headache), intracerebral, extradural and subdural (head trauma, anticoagulants).
  • Secondary: meningitis and encephalitis (fever, rash, confusion, seizures), stroke or TIA (focal deficits), temporal arteritis (over 50, jaw claudication), angle-closure glaucoma (red eye, halos), trigeminal neuralgia, shingles, medication overuse, hypertensive crisis, tumour (morning headache, worse on coughing, weight loss) and trauma.

Other causes of thunderclap headache worth knowing are reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (often after exertion or sex, or with vasoactive drugs), cervical artery dissection, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and pituitary apoplexy.

Investigations

  • Non-contrast CT brain is the first test and is most sensitive within the first 6 hours. If it is negative and SAH is still suspected, an LP looks for xanthochromia (at least 12 hours after onset) or a CT angiogram is done, depending on local protocol.
  • No LP for Clark: his CT is diagnostic, and an LP with raised intracranial pressure (reduced GCS, hydrocephalus) risks herniation.
  • CT angiography finds the aneurysm and plans treatment. CTA should not be delayed for a creatinine result. At eGFR 70 the contrast carries a low risk of kidney injury; repeat creatinine at 24–48 hours.
  • Bloods: FBC, UEC, LFTs, coagulation and group and hold. His results show no coagulopathy, a renal baseline in keeping with his ADPKD and a stress leucocytosis. His sodium of 138 is a baseline; check it daily, because hyponatraemia is common after SAH.

Grading

The World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grade uses GCS and motor deficit: grade II is GCS 13 to 14 without a deficit, and grade IV is GCS 7 to 12. Clark arrived at grade II and fell to grade IV as hydrocephalus developed. A worse grade predicts a worse outcome, but much of his decline can be reversed with an EVD.

Interpreting the deterioration

At 15:25 his GCS fell by 2 points, his HR fell to 48 and his SBP rose to 204, with irregular breathing. That is Cushing's triad (hypertension with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respiration), a late sign of raised intracranial pressure before coning. Under Between the Flags, a GCS fall of 2 or more points is a rapid response call. The rise in BP is compensating to keep cerebral perfusion pressure up. The fix is to lower the intracranial pressure (an EVD), not to drop the BP aggressively.

Management (eTG Neurology)

  • ABCDE assessment and early senior help (in the ED, the ED consultant or registrar to the bedside and a move to resus). Intubate if the GCS falls to 8 or less or he cannot protect his airway.
  • Urgent neurosurgical referral: an EVD for acute hydrocephalus, and early securing of the aneurysm by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping to prevent rebleeding.
  • Monitoring: bed rest with the head up 30°, neurological observations (GCS and pupils) with BP, HR, RR and temperature, and cardiac monitoring. Osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) only as directed by neurosurgery.
  • Blood pressure: control to the target set by neurosurgery or ICU until the aneurysm is secured, avoiding hypotension.
  • Nimodipine 60 mg orally (or via a nasogastric tube) 4-hourly for 21 days reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm. Withhold his amlodipine, a second dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that adds to the risk of hypotension when his cerebral perfusion depends on his BP. If BP falls, give nimodipine 30 mg 2-hourly (per eTG) rather than stopping it.
  • Supportive care: paracetamol and carefully titrated opioid, an antiemetic, isotonic fluids to keep him euvolaemic (avoid hypotonic fluids and fluid restriction), stool softeners to avoid straining, and mechanical VTE prophylaxis until the aneurysm is secured.
  • ADPKD: avoid nephrotoxins, especially NSAIDs (which also raise bleeding risk), keep him euvolaemic and repeat creatinine 24–48 hours after the contrast load.

Complications and safety netting

The pre-terminal complication is raised intracranial pressure with herniation. Nurses escalate any fall in GCS, pupil asymmetry, new focal signs, seizures, a sudden worse headache or vomiting (rebleeding, highest risk in the first day), bradycardia, BP above target, and irregular breathing. Over the following 2 weeks watch for hydrocephalus, delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (days 3 to 14: new confusion or focal deficit), hyponatraemia (from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting; check sodium daily), seizures, and cardiac effects such as ECG changes and stunned myocardium.

After recovery he needs neurosurgical follow-up with aneurysm imaging, rehabilitation, tight BP control, and a driving review before he drives again. His father and aunt have ADPKD and now there is an aneurysmal SAH in the family, so the renal team discusses aneurysm screening for relatives with ADPKD and genetic counselling for his children.
points: A thunderclap headache, maximal within seconds to a minute, is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Always ask about an earlier 'warning' headache, which is often mistaken for migraine.
ADPKD and hypertension are risk factors for intracranial berry aneurysms. Ask about the past history and family history in every severe headache.
Non-contrast CT brain is the first test. An LP is only for a suspected SAH with a negative CT, and never when the GCS is reduced or the CT shows hydrocephalus. CT angiography finds the aneurysm.

A rising BP, a falling heart rate and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad), with a falling GCS, mean raised intracranial pressure and impending coning. Call a rapid response and an urgent neurosurgeon for an EVD, and do not chase the BP down.

Acute management: airway protection if needed, early neurosurgery to secure the aneurysm, head up 30° with neurological observations, nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days, euvolaemia, analgesia, an antiemetic and stool softeners.
Watch for rebleeding, hydrocephalus, delayed cerebral ischaemia (days 3 to 14), hyponatraemia and seizures. Avoid NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins in kidney disease.
